extraction.body: Muse’s traction is surging, fueled by Meta’s promotion of the AI app at its annual Meta Connect developer conference this week and strong early reviews that praised its polished design and highly capable AI model under the hood. At the start of the week, Muse had surpassed 2.5 million downloads since its September 8 launch. Now the app has amassed more than 3.4 million downloads, according to the most recent estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower . The install numbers are only current as of the firm’s Thursday estimates, which can lag behind real-world adoption. That means they don’t even capture the full impact of the big push Muse received at Meta Connect, where the social network company announced a range of upcoming features for the new AI app, including video chat with the Muse avatar, support for computer use on the Mac, a dedicated email address, more partners and connectors, and plans for smart glasses integrations. Estimates from other market intelligence firms show Muse with similarly strong traction, though their numbers vary quite a bit. Apptopia , for example, puts Muse’s total number of downloads to date at 4.3 million. (Muse is currently only available in the U.S. and Canada). It estimates that 2.6 million of those were on iOS alone. Meanwhile, another firm, Appfigures , says it sees Muse installs at roughly 2.3 million as of Thursday, almost evenly split between iOS and Android. Sensor Tower also has visibility into daily active users for the Muse app following the Meta Connect conference. It found that figure climbed 27% on Wednesday after the event wrapped. Before the conference, Muse was already off to a strong start. Sensor Tower said the app reached an estimated 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks on the app stores. During that time (September 8 to September 17), the Muse app averaged 55% day-over-day growth in downloads. For comparison, ChatGPT averaged 24% day-over-day download growth in its first 10 days after launch. Download growth for Claude and Grok, meanwhile, declined during their respective launches. On Friday, September 18, Muse climbed to the top of the U.S. App Store and has retained its ranking ever since. It also reached the top spot on the Google Play Store on September 19 and remains there today. While much of Muse’s traction so far is organic, the app is also benefiting from the same cross-platform promotion that helped one of Meta’s latest social apps, Instagram Threads, top 500 million monthly active users — that is, Meta is marketing the app to existing Facebook and Instagram users. passages: As reports of OpenAI’s models breaking containment, hacking sites, and generally getting out of control pile up, the company has made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models.

extraction.body: As reports of OpenAI’s models breaking containment, hacking sites, and generally getting out of control pile up, the company has made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models. The decision was made after a model being tested within a sandbox exploited a loophole to gain internet access. The incident happened on September 20th, and “All training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use” remains paused as of Saturday evening, September 25th. In addition, OpenAI revealed on Friday that its agents had inappropriately uploaded 53nimages from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. The company has not stated if the images were AI-generated, photos, or contained identifiable people. As it dug into its records, following the Hugging Face hack, it’s uncovered more and more instances of “unexpected or concerning behavior.” It’s evidence not just of how difficult AI agents are becoming to control as they grow more advanced, but also of the challenge of tracking their actions.

extraction.body: As reports of OpenAI’s models breaking containment, hacking sites, and generally getting out of control pile up, the company has made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models. The decision was made after a model being tested within a sandbox exploited a loophole to gain internet access. The incident happened on September 20th, and “All training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use” remains paused as of Saturday evening, September 25th. In addition, OpenAI revealed on Friday that its agents had inappropriately uploaded 53nimages from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. The company has not stated if the images were AI-generated, photos, or contained identifiable people. As it dug into its records, following the Hugging Face hack, it’s uncovered more and more instances of “unexpected or concerning behavior.” It’s evidence not just of how difficult AI agents are becoming to control as they grow more advanced, but also of the challenge of tracking their actions.

extraction.body: Hospitals’ use of artificial intelligence tools as they submit insurance claims led to an additional $942 million in healthcare spending over a two-year period, according to an analysis by the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association . The BCBSA analysis found “a sharp increase in patients being documented as having complex conditions,” but argued there is a “clear disconnect between [medical] coding and treatment,” as there’s “no evidence of corresponding change in care delivered.” The New York Times pointed the analysis as just the latest sign that AI is contributing to an increase in healthcare costs . While battles between hospitals and insurers over treatments and payments are nothing new, the NYT said the use of AI on both sides seems to be making it worse. Dr. Shiv Rao, founder of AI startup Abridge, acknowledged that the use of AI could lead to “a horrible dystopic future nobody wants to live in,” with “bots fighting bots, agents fighting agents.” But Rao said it might also reduce tensions and cut costs. And the BCBSA’s senior vice president Luke Chalker resisted characterizing the situation as a battle, claiming, “It’s not a war. It’s a completely one-sided blood bath,” with insurers on the losing side.

extraction.body: A federal jury in San Diego awarded Taction Technology more than $5.7 billion in damages Friday after finding that Apple infringed claims from two haptics patents. Taction sued Apple in 2021 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. The company alleged that Apple was improperly "capitalizing on Taction's innovation and success" by selling devices that infringed on its vibration technology, according to the complaint . Apple initially won dismissal in 2023, and the Federal Circuit later revived the case. "While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," Apple told CNBC in a statement. "Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction's technology, and we will appeal." "We're happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights," the company's lead counsel, Lance Yang, partner at Quinn Emanuel, told CNBC. "Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming." The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input. Taction argued that Apple's "Taptic Engine," which is embedded in its Apple Watches and iPhones, uses its inventions without proper license or authority. The jury trial began Sept. 14, and the seven jurors deliberated for two days after proceedings concluded. They returned at 1:15 p.m. PT on Friday and delivered the verdict in favor of Taction. Apple is currently on the hook for a record-breaking patent infringement case, after a federal jury decided that the iPhone maker has to pay more than $5.7 billion to Taction, a San Diego-based company that produces audio and gaming peripherals with haptic feedback. If the decision holds, it would be one of the largest patent infringement case payouts in the US, topping an ongoing case involving Intel for $3 billion. Taction filed the lawsuit back in 2021, alleging that Apple's Taptic Engine found in its various iPhone and Apple Watch models infringed on two of its patents related to haptic feedback. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2023 by a federal judge in San Diego, but later brought back into the courts following a decision by the US ​Court ⁠of Appeals for the Federal Circuit a couple of years later. The latest jury verdict from Friday said that Apple unintentionally infringed on two of Taction's patents. According to Bloomberg Law , Apple didn't agree with the jury's decision nor the damages and would appeal the verdict. Before the Taction lawsuit, Apple was previously hit with another patent infringement lawsuit from Immersion. The company filed a complaint against Apple, also accusing it of patent violations with haptic tech found in iPhones, Apple Watches and MacBooks, but eventually settled for an undisclosed amount. More notably, Apple is in the midst of another patent infringement battle surrounding its Apple Watch and a feature that tracks blood-oxygen levels. In November, another federal jury ruled that Apple has to pay $634 million for violation patents from Masimo, but the tech giant is similarly planning to appeal this jury verdict.

While the 157-page report from the Illinois-based Lake Forest Group found no evidence UVU employees or agents acted in “bad faith or in willing and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” it does reveal serious security “gaps” and a failure of UVU officials to follow their own policies.

“UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature,” Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to The Federalist.
On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states.

More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements.

extraction.body: ‘UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared,’ an attorney for the slain conservative icon’s family said. Utah Valley University failed on a number of fronts to protect Charlie Kirk from the assassin who took his life at an outdoor event a little over a year ago, according to an independent review released on Friday. While the 157-page report from the Illinois-based Lake Forest Group found no evidence UVU employees or agents acted in “bad faith or in willing and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” it does reveal serious security “gaps” and a failure of UVU officials to follow their own policies. The “After-Action Report,” according to the Kirk family, reaffirms the facts laid out in the family’s recent notice of impending legal action: The university’s security failures rendered the conservative icon “helpless to the rooftop shooter in an assassination that could have been avoided.” “UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature,” Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to The Federalist. “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie.” The university did not respond to The Federalist’s follow-up questions, but UVU President Jon Anderson released a brief statement. “Our commitment does not end with this report,” Anderson said. “Its findings will guide our continued safety efforts as we move forward together with care, civility, and resilience.” The report details the day the Turning Point USA founder was murdered in front of some 3,000 spectators, including his wife and young children. It also delves into the preparations for Kirk’s UVU appearance, the first stop on his nationwide tour of college campuses that he billed as The American Comeback Tour . In their notice of claim, the Kirk family notes the university assigned “only six campus police officers,” or a quarter of the full UVU police force to the outdoor event. UVU Police chief Jeff Long, according to the notice, had sought approval from then-university President Astrid Tuminez, but the request was denied. Originally, police staffing included just three officers — the chief, a patrol officer, and a reserve officer, according to the review. “After observing the size of the crowd, Chief Long requested that a uniformed UVUPD detective assist, as well as an additional officer and a sergeant,” the review states. Two plainclothes officers from Utah State University were also on hand, but in an observational capacity. The Turning Point USA event was scheduled to take place at Utah State later in the month. The review notes concerns “regarding UVUPD staffing levels, training, structure, organizational placement, and visibility within the universities’s leadership framework.” It recommends the police department consider whether staffing plans “provide sufficient fixed-post coverage and mobile response capacity.” “Staffing limitations should be addressed through advanced planning, mutual aid agreements, and coordination with nearby law enforcement partners or university police agencies,” the report advises. The consultants recommend UVU conduct a formal staffing analysis. Public safety partners — including local, state, and federal officers — responded quickly following the shooting, the review found. But the attack also exposed gaps in mutual aid. UVU had access to myriad outside resources, “but those resources were not fully integrated into pre-event planning.” Technology, or the failure to use it, was also a problem. On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states. “Similarly, the broader, physical security technology environment would benefit for more integrated workflows that connect alarms, video, access control, mapping, notification, and dispatch response,” the consultants advise. The report does note the surveillance system proved valuable after the shooting. Law enforcement officials were able to use the footage to track the suspect and ultimately charge Tyler Robinson, Kirk’s alleged assassin. A review of footage during Robinson’s preliminary hearing showed the shooter “running across the roof” of the UVU building above the courtyard to a “sniper’s nest.” “If such footage had been monitored in real-time, Kirk’s tragic death could have been avoided,” the notice of claim asserts, adding that the campus police department could have used drones to secure the rooftops and sprawling venue. The review notes that omission as well. More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements. “A site-specific coordination meeting involving UVUPD protection detail should have occurred several days before the event to assess vulnerabilities, clarify responsibilities, and determine whether available personnel and resources were sufficient to support the security plan,” the report states. The report also notes planning flaws with Kirk’s private security team. But the overarching problem was that the university failed to fully take into account the challenges associated with securing a large-scale outdoor event with a “high-profile speaker” and anticipated protests. It does note that UVU offered alternate locations to hold the event, including interior sites. The headline in Friday’s Salt Lake Tribune declares, “Utah Valley University tried to warn Charlie Kirk’s staff of risks, but team ignored concerns.” The UVU-friendly piece notes that university staff suggested a few weeks before the event that Turning Point move it to a more secure location. “The organization, though, insisted on having it in the open campus courtyard,” the news outlet asserts. Ultimately, university officials went ahead with the outdoor plan. It shouldn’t have, according to the review. “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control, and other conditions necessary to support campus safety,” the report states. “The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement,” Parkinson, the Kirk family lawyer, said in the statement. “Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.” © 2026 The Federalist, A wholly independent division of FDRLST Media. The university did not respond to The Federalist’s follow-up questions, but UVU President Jon Anderson released a brief statement.
“Our commitment does not end with this report,” Anderson said. “Its findings will guide our continued safety efforts as we move forward together with care, civility, and resilience.”

The report details the day the Turning Point USA founder was murdered in front of some 3,000 spectators, including his wife and young children. “After observing the size of the crowd, Chief Long requested that a uniformed UVUPD detective assist, as well as an additional officer and a sergeant,” the review states. Two plainclothes officers from Utah State University were also on hand, but in an observational capacity. The Turning Point USA event was scheduled to take place at Utah State later in the month.

The review notes concerns “regarding UVUPD staffing levels, training, structure, organizational placement, and visibility within the universities’s leadership framework.” It recommends the police department consider whether staffing plans “provide sufficient fixed-post coverage and mobile response capacity.”

“Staffing limitations should be addressed through advanced planning, mutual aid agreements, and coordination with nearby law enforcement partners or university police agencies,” the report advises. The consultants recommend UVU conduct a formal staffing analysis.

Public safety partners — including local, state, and federal officers — responded quickly following the shooting, the review found. But the attack also exposed gaps in mutual aid. UVU had access to myriad outside resources, “but those resources were not fully integrated into pre-event planning.”

Technology, or the failure to use it, was also a problem. On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states.

“Similarly, the broader, physical security technology environment would benefit for more integrated workflows that connect alarms, video, access control, mapping, notification, and dispatch response,” the consultants advise.

The report does note the surveillance system proved valuable after the shooting. Law enforcement officials were able to use the footage to track the suspect and ultimately charge Tyler Robinson, Kirk’s alleged assassin.
A review of footage during Robinson’s preliminary hearing showed the shooter “running across the roof” of the UVU building above the courtyard to a “sniper’s nest.”

“If such footage had been monitored in real-time, Kirk’s tragic death could have been avoided,” the notice of claim asserts, adding that the campus police department could have used drones to secure the rooftops and sprawling venue. The review notes that omission as well.

More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements.

“A site-specific coordination meeting involving UVUPD protection detail should have occurred several days before the event to assess vulnerabilities, clarify responsibilities, and determine whether available personnel and resources were sufficient to support the security plan,” the report states.

The report also notes planning flaws with Kirk’s private security team. But the overarching problem was that the university failed to fully take into account the challenges associated with securing a large-scale outdoor event with a “high-profile speaker” and anticipated protests. It does note that UVU offered alternate locations to hold the event, including interior sites.

The headline in Friday’s Salt Lake Tribune declares, “Utah Valley University tried to warn Charlie Kirk’s staff of risks, but team ignored concerns.” The UVU-friendly piece notes that university staff suggested a few weeks before the event that Turning Point move it to a more secure location. “The organization, though, insisted on having it in the open campus courtyard,” the news outlet asserts.
Ultimately, university officials went ahead with the outdoor plan. It shouldn’t have, according to the review.

“UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control, and other conditions necessary to support campus safety,” the report states.

passages: At Utah Valley University, fostering a safe and supportive learning environment is one of our highest priorities.

Following the assassination of Charlie Kirk on September 10, 2025, UVU commissioned an independent external review to examine the university’s planning, preparedness, response, and recovery and identify opportunities to enhance campus safety.
It also recognized the strength of the response by public safety partners and meaningful steps UVU has taken since the tragedy.
The review was conducted by a consortium of independent experts from Robert L.
The review calls for documented assessments and earlier, more structured coordination with private security teams and law enforcement partners for major events.

The project team combined legal, operational, and investigative expertise in law enforcement, campus safety, physical security, executive protection, emergency preparedness, threat assessment, and crisis communications.

While we’ve made meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year, this review provides additional recommendations that will continue to guide our work as we move forward with care, civility, and resilience.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Utah Valley University failed on a number of fronts to protect Charlie Kirk from the assassin who took his life at an outdoor event a little over a year ago, according to an independent review released on Friday.

While the 157-page report from the Illinois-based Lake Forest Group found no evidence UVU employees or agents acted in “bad faith or in willing and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” it does reveal serious security “gaps” and a failure of UVU officials to follow their own policies.

“UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature,” Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to The Federalist.
On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states.

More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements.
At Utah Valley University, fostering a safe and supportive learning environment is one of our highest priorities.

Following the assassination of Charlie Kirk on September 10, 2025, UVU commissioned an independent external review to examine the university’s planning, preparedness, response, and recovery and identify opportunities to enhance campus safety.
It also recognized the strength of the response by public safety partners and meaningful steps UVU has taken since the tragedy.
The review was conducted by a consortium of independent experts from Robert L.
The review calls for documented assessments and earlier, more structured coordination with private security teams and law enforcement partners for major events.

The project team combined legal, operational, and investigative expertise in law enforcement, campus safety, physical security, executive protection, emergency preparedness, threat assessment, and crisis communications.

The review found UVU had existing campus safety policies, personnel and resources but needed more consistent implementation, clearer responsibilities and stronger coordination during large events and emergencies.

The university also said it was requiring additional safety training, strengthening event security planning and ticketing procedures, and increasing coordination with outside law enforcement agencies. “September 10 will always be part of UVU’s history, but it will not define our future,” UVU President Jon Anderson said. “Our responsibility is to care for our community, learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations.” A group of independent safety, law enforcement and legal experts conducted the review.

Okay, don’t put anything out on that,” said Burbank.To address that, UVU announced that it’s created a chief public safety officer position to coordinate campus police and emergency response — while also implementing many of the review’s recommendations.For those who still have that day on their minds, they hope it can be a positive way to move forward from such a tragic moment in the school’s history.“It’s going to be hard to make people feel safe again at events, like I still have people talking about it in classes,” said Lowe.

extraction.body: ‘UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared,’ an attorney for the slain conservative icon’s family said. Utah Valley University failed on a number of fronts to protect Charlie Kirk from the assassin who took his life at an outdoor event a little over a year ago, according to an independent review released on Friday. While the 157-page report from the Illinois-based Lake Forest Group found no evidence UVU employees or agents acted in “bad faith or in willing and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” it does reveal serious security “gaps” and a failure of UVU officials to follow their own policies. The “After-Action Report,” according to the Kirk family, reaffirms the facts laid out in the family’s recent notice of impending legal action: The university’s security failures rendered the conservative icon “helpless to the rooftop shooter in an assassination that could have been avoided.” “UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature,” Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to The Federalist. “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie.” The university did not respond to The Federalist’s follow-up questions, but UVU President Jon Anderson released a brief statement. “Our commitment does not end with this report,” Anderson said. “Its findings will guide our continued safety efforts as we move forward together with care, civility, and resilience.” The report details the day the Turning Point USA founder was murdered in front of some 3,000 spectators, including his wife and young children. It also delves into the preparations for Kirk’s UVU appearance, the first stop on his nationwide tour of college campuses that he billed as The American Comeback Tour . In their notice of claim, the Kirk family notes the university assigned “only six campus police officers,” or a quarter of the full UVU police force to the outdoor event. UVU Police chief Jeff Long, according to the notice, had sought approval from then-university President Astrid Tuminez, but the request was denied. Originally, police staffing included just three officers — the chief, a patrol officer, and a reserve officer, according to the review. “After observing the size of the crowd, Chief Long requested that a uniformed UVUPD detective assist, as well as an additional officer and a sergeant,” the review states. Two plainclothes officers from Utah State University were also on hand, but in an observational capacity. The Turning Point USA event was scheduled to take place at Utah State later in the month. The review notes concerns “regarding UVUPD staffing levels, training, structure, organizational placement, and visibility within the universities’s leadership framework.” It recommends the police department consider whether staffing plans “provide sufficient fixed-post coverage and mobile response capacity.” “Staffing limitations should be addressed through advanced planning, mutual aid agreements, and coordination with nearby law enforcement partners or university police agencies,” the report advises. The consultants recommend UVU conduct a formal staffing analysis. Public safety partners — including local, state, and federal officers — responded quickly following the shooting, the review found. But the attack also exposed gaps in mutual aid. UVU had access to myriad outside resources, “but those resources were not fully integrated into pre-event planning.” Technology, or the failure to use it, was also a problem. On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states. “Similarly, the broader, physical security technology environment would benefit for more integrated workflows that connect alarms, video, access control, mapping, notification, and dispatch response,” the consultants advise. The report does note the surveillance system proved valuable after the shooting. Law enforcement officials were able to use the footage to track the suspect and ultimately charge Tyler Robinson, Kirk’s alleged assassin. A review of footage during Robinson’s preliminary hearing showed the shooter “running across the roof” of the UVU building above the courtyard to a “sniper’s nest.” “If such footage had been monitored in real-time, Kirk’s tragic death could have been avoided,” the notice of claim asserts, adding that the campus police department could have used drones to secure the rooftops and sprawling venue. The review notes that omission as well. More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements. “A site-specific coordination meeting involving UVUPD protection detail should have occurred several days before the event to assess vulnerabilities, clarify responsibilities, and determine whether available personnel and resources were sufficient to support the security plan,” the report states. The report also notes planning flaws with Kirk’s private security team. But the overarching problem was that the university failed to fully take into account the challenges associated with securing a large-scale outdoor event with a “high-profile speaker” and anticipated protests. It does note that UVU offered alternate locations to hold the event, including interior sites. The headline in Friday’s Salt Lake Tribune declares, “Utah Valley University tried to warn Charlie Kirk’s staff of risks, but team ignored concerns.” The UVU-friendly piece notes that university staff suggested a few weeks before the event that Turning Point move it to a more secure location. “The organization, though, insisted on having it in the open campus courtyard,” the news outlet asserts. Ultimately, university officials went ahead with the outdoor plan. It shouldn’t have, according to the review. “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control, and other conditions necessary to support campus safety,” the report states. “The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement,” Parkinson, the Kirk family lawyer, said in the statement. “Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.” © 2026 The Federalist, A wholly independent division of FDRLST Media. Our responsibility is to care for our community, learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations. This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn. While we’ve made meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year, this review provides additional recommendations that will continue to guide our work as we move forward with care, civility, and resilience.” The independent external review identified a foundation of campus safety policies, personnel, and resources, along with inconsistencies in how those capabilities were put into practice before and during the September 10 event. It also recognized the strength of the response by public safety partners and meaningful steps UVU has taken since the tragedy. The review also documented the planning and coordination leading up to September 10, including the following: The report’s timeline also documents communication between UVUPD and TPUSA began on September 3. Then on September 8, TPUSA’s security team raised a concern about access to the elevated Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway above the area where Kirk would speak and requested access controls. On the morning of September 10, TPUSA’s security team again raised concerns about people on the walkway. Chief Long responded that officers would arrive by 11:00 a.m. to address the request. UVUPD officers cleared the area by directing people away from the area directly above the speaking location and blocked it off with police tape. The UVUPD Chief of Police proposed meeting with TPUSA’s security at 11:00 a.m. on the walkway above the canopy where Charlie Kirk would speak, but this meeting did not occur. A detailed timeline and verbatim text exchanges are included in the full report. Beyond documenting the sequence of events, the review examined UVU’s planning, preparedness, response, and recovery and identified key findings. “It is the opinion of the Project Team, based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others.” — After-Action Report for Utah Valley University The summaries below introduce 10 key findings, while the full report provides the supporting analysis and recommendations. Formalize security planning for high-profile events While a UVU committee and a TPUSA field representative engaged in a planning meeting, the September 10 event lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or event action plan. The review recommends a more structured planning framework that addresses venue selection, attendance, staffing, access, communications, and emergency response before key event decisions are finalized. Strengthen protective planning and coordination for outdoor venues Planning for the event did not formalize assessments of elevated vantage points, building access, and other site-specific security concerns. The review calls for documented assessments and earlier, more structured coordination with private security teams and law enforcement partners for major events. Both TPUSA security and UVUPD failed to ensure a joint pre-event briefing and security walk-through occurred. Reviewers found this was a critical missed opportunity to identify security concerns, clarify responsibilities, and coordinate protective measures. Since September 10, 2025, UVU has taken proactive steps to learn from events surrounding the assassination of Charlie Kirk. The reviewers recognized meaningful progress in community support, crisis communication planning, emergency preparedness, notification practices, and coordination with public safety partners. “UVU’s post-incident efforts reflect meaningful progress in several areas.” — After-Action Report for Utah Valley University The reviewers examined not only the planning and response leading up to and on September 10, but also UVU’s broader event planning, safety, and security processes. As a result, some recommendations in the review reflect practices that UVU had already implemented before September 10 or had already begun enhancing. These recommendations were included to reinforce the importance of continuing those efforts and maintaining strong event planning and security practices. UVU has already implemented, is currently implementing, or is actively working toward many of the review’s recommendations. The following recommendations are areas in which UVU had already taken action, has since taken action, or is in the process of taking action: Action Items Completed or Underway for Organizational Alignment, Staffing, Training and Professional Standards Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Planning, Response, and Interagency Coordination Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Security Planning and Security Assessment Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Security Operations Action Items Completed or Underway for Access Control, Screening and Credentialing Action Items Completed or Underway for Behavioral Threat Assessment and Threat Management Action Items Completed or Underway for Post-Incident Recovery, Corrective Actions and Preparedness Enhancements Action Items Completed or Underway for Legal Considerations Our commitment does not end with the release of this report. We will continue to communicate progress as recommendations are evaluated and implemented and use training and exercises to assess how these changes work in practice. The review was conducted by a consortium of independent experts from Robert L. Davis LLC, Doherty Advisory LLC, The Lake Forest Group, and Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, LLP. The project team performed site visits, conducted more than 70 interviews and examined thousands of pages of university policies, training materials, operational records, digital evidence, and dispatch and communication records. The project team combined legal, operational, and investigative expertise in law enforcement, campus safety, physical security, executive protection, emergency preparedness, threat assessment, and crisis communications. The findings and recommendations are those of the independent project team.

The UVUPD Chief of Police proposed meeting with TPUSA’s security at 11:00 a.m. on the walkway above the canopy where Charlie Kirk would speak, but this meeting did not occur. A detailed timeline and verbatim text exchanges are included in the full report.
Beyond documenting the sequence of events, the review examined UVU’s planning, preparedness, response, and recovery and identified key findings.

“It is the opinion of the Project Team, based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others.”
— After-Action Report for Utah Valley University
The summaries below introduce 10 key findings, while the full report provides the supporting analysis and recommendations.

Formalize security planning for high-profile events While a UVU committee and a TPUSA field representative engaged in a planning meeting, the September 10 event lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or event action plan.

The review recommends a more structured planning framework that addresses venue selection, attendance, staffing, access, communications, and emergency response before key event decisions are finalized.

Strengthen protective planning and coordination for outdoor venues Planning for the event did not formalize assessments of elevated vantage points, building access, and other site-specific security concerns. The review calls for documented assessments and earlier, more structured coordination with private security teams and law enforcement partners for major events.

Both TPUSA security and UVUPD failed to ensure a joint pre-event briefing and security walk-through occurred. Reviewers found this was a critical missed opportunity to identify security concerns, clarify responsibilities, and coordinate protective measures.

Since September 10, 2025, UVU has taken proactive steps to learn from events surrounding the assassination of Charlie Kirk. The reviewers recognized meaningful progress in community support, crisis communication planning, emergency preparedness, notification practices, and coordination with public safety partners.
“UVU’s post-incident efforts reflect meaningful progress in several areas.”
— After-Action Report for Utah Valley University

The reviewers examined not only the planning and response leading up to and on September 10, but also UVU’s broader event planning, safety, and security processes. As a result, some recommendations in the review reflect practices that UVU had already implemented before September 10 or had already begun enhancing. These recommendations were included to reinforce the importance of continuing those efforts and maintaining strong event planning and security practices.

UVU has already implemented, is currently implementing, or is actively working toward many of the review’s recommendations. The following recommendations are areas in which UVU had already taken action, has since taken action, or is in the process of taking action:
Action Items Completed or Underway for Organizational Alignment, Staffing, Training and Professional Standards
Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Planning, Response, and Interagency Coordination
Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Security Planning and Security Assessment
Action Items Completed or Underway for Event Security Operations
Action Items Completed or Underway for Access Control, Screening and Credentialing
Action Items Completed or Underway for Behavioral Threat Assessment and Threat Management
Action Items Completed or Underway for Post-Incident Recovery, Corrective Actions and Preparedness Enhancements
Action Items Completed or Underway for Legal Considerations

Our commitment does not end with the release of this report. We will continue to communicate progress as recommendations are evaluated and implemented and use training and exercises to assess how these changes work in practice.

The review was conducted by a consortium of independent experts from Robert L. Davis LLC, Doherty Advisory LLC, The Lake Forest Group, and Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, LLP. The project team performed site visits, conducted more than 70 interviews and examined thousands of pages of university policies, training materials, operational records, digital evidence, and dispatch and communication records.

The project team combined legal, operational, and investigative expertise in law enforcement, campus safety, physical security, executive protection, emergency preparedness, threat assessment, and crisis communications. The findings and recommendations are those of the independent project team.

facts.text: Utah Valley University failed on a number of fronts to protect Charlie Kirk from the assassin who took his life at an outdoor event a little over a year ago, according to an independent review released on Friday.

While the 157-page report from the Illinois-based Lake Forest Group found no evidence UVU employees or agents acted in “bad faith or in willing and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” it does reveal serious security “gaps” and a failure of UVU officials to follow their own policies.

“UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature,” Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to The Federalist.
On the day of Kirk’s assassination, “no individual had been specifically assigned to monitor relevant camera feeds in real-time for event security purposes,” the report states.

More broadly, the review found that university officials lacked a comprehensive written security assessment or an action plan, which would have laid out staffing assignments, post responsibilities, mutual aid resources and several other critical security elements.
At Utah Valley University, fostering a safe and supportive learning environment is one of our highest priorities.

Following the assassination of Charlie Kirk on September 10, 2025, UVU commissioned an independent external review to examine the university’s planning, preparedness, response, and recovery and identify opportunities to enhance campus safety.
It also recognized the strength of the response by public safety partners and meaningful steps UVU has taken since the tragedy.
The review was conducted by a consortium of independent experts from Robert L.
The review calls for documented assessments and earlier, more structured coordination with private security teams and law enforcement partners for major events.

The project team combined legal, operational, and investigative expertise in law enforcement, campus safety, physical security, executive protection, emergency preparedness, threat assessment, and crisis communications.

The review found UVU had existing campus safety policies, personnel and resources but needed more consistent implementation, clearer responsibilities and stronger coordination during large events and emergencies.

The university also said it was requiring additional safety training, strengthening event security planning and ticketing procedures, and increasing coordination with outside law enforcement agencies. “September 10 will always be part of UVU’s history, but it will not define our future,” UVU President Jon Anderson said. “Our responsibility is to care for our community, learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations.” A group of independent safety, law enforcement and legal experts conducted the review.
The university said the external review found no UVU employee or agent acted in bad faith or showed willful disregard for others’ safety before or after the shooting.

The team conducted site visits, interviewed more than 70 people and reviewed thousands of pages of university policies, training materials, records, digital evidence, and dispatch and communication records, UVU said.

passages: Apple just took a massive legal hit, with a federal jury awarding Taction Technology more than $5.7 billion in damages for patent infringement related to haptic feedback technology in iPhones and Apple Watches.
This massive patent verdict against Apple signals a new chapter in tech patent warfare, where specialized firms are successfully targeting the core technologies that define user experiences.
The verdict represents one of the largest patent awards in tech history and immediately puts Apple's legal team on high alert as the company vows to appeal.
From the iPhone's home button replacement to the Apple Watch's Digital Crown, haptic technology has become integral to the Apple user experience that the company markets as uniquely intuitive.
The company's focused approach to haptic patents mirrors successful strategies used by other patent holders who've secured massive settlements from Apple, Google, and Microsoft in recent years.

Taction Technology, which has been quietly building its patent portfolio around haptic innovations, successfully convinced jurors that Apple's Taptic Engine and related feedback systems infringe on their proprietary technology.
This verdict also highlights the growing importance of haptic technology patents in an industry where physical buttons are disappearing.
Patent experts note that while massive jury awards often get reduced on appeal, the size of this verdict suggests Taction presented compelling evidence of infringement.
While Apple's appeal will likely drag on for years, the case has already sent shockwaves through an industry increasingly dependent on haptic feedback.

extraction.body: A federal jury in San Diego awarded Taction Technology more than $5.7 billion in damages Friday after finding that Apple infringed claims from two haptics patents. Taction sued Apple in 2021 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. The company alleged that Apple was improperly "capitalizing on Taction's innovation and success" by selling devices that infringed on its vibration technology, according to the complaint . Apple initially won dismissal in 2023, and the Federal Circuit later revived the case. "While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," Apple told CNBC in a statement. "Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction's technology, and we will appeal." "We're happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights," the company's lead counsel, Lance Yang, partner at Quinn Emanuel, told CNBC. "Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming." The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input. Taction argued that Apple's "Taptic Engine," which is embedded in its Apple Watches and iPhones, uses its inventions without proper license or authority. The jury trial began Sept. 14, and the seven jurors deliberated for two days after proceedings concluded. They returned at 1:15 p.m. PT on Friday and delivered the verdict in favor of Taction. sources.title: Google tests buying from Walmart-owned Flipkart through Gemini and AI Mode in India
passages: Google has started testing a way for shoppers in India to buy products from Walmart-owned Flipkart directly through Gemini and AI Mode, as the search giant looks to expand its AI services from product discovery into transactions.
Earlier this year, it introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) as an open standard designed to let AI agents interact with retailers across the shopping journey, including checkout.
The company has since expanded UCP with other capabilities, including allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s site to complete a purchase.
The early test is limited to some users and a small selection of products, including smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, the people told TechCrunch.

Earlier this month, Google said Flipkart was among the merchants partnering with it to bring what it calls “agentic” shopping experiences to consumers in India, but it had not disclosed details of the test or its rollout timeline.
Google plans to roll out the experience more broadly later in October, ahead of India’s festive shopping season, one of the people said.

Asked about the Flipkart test, a Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the company is “always testing new features and experiences to help people discover and connect with businesses more easily.” The company regularly runs experiments and has no further details to share, the spokesperson added.
Notably, Google has a financial relationship with Flipkart — alongside its technology partnership with the e-commerce company.
It brings up a Flipkart-branded checkout flow when a user taps the Buy button.
It is not clear what technology powers the test.
India, the world’s second-largest internet market with more than a billion internet subscribers, sees Flipkart and Amazon compete fiercely for online shoppers.
For now, the Buy option is not appearing across all retailers surfaced by Google’s AI services.
In the experience seen by TechCrunch, listings from rivals including Amazon appeared alongside Flipkart products but did not offer the option to purchase directly through the AI interface.
Jagmeet covers startups, tech policy-related updates, and all other major tech-centric developments from India for TechCrunch.
He previously worked as a principal correspondent at NDTV.

The test comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI are adding commerce capabilities to their AI offerings, striving to move beyond answering shopping queries and recommending products to playing a more direct role in online purchases.

Boeing's initial bulletin told airlines a software fix would be ready sometime in 2028 and it would issue updated guidance about procedures for pilots to follow in November.
It is notable that several U.S. airlines appear to be taking a trust-but-verify approach to Boeing on the issue, having been stung by groundings and delays due to previous Boeing mistakes on the Max.

The Max 7 was certified with software version 14, while the Max 10 was using version 14.1 during its certification testing.

The software glitch was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

In rare circumstances where there is a missed approach — and where a pilot is using a precision approach with autopilot engaged and makes changes to their pre-programmed flight plan — an issue with the flight management computer could cause the plane's vertical navigation system, known as VNAV, to disengage and transition to a less sophisticated level of automated pitch control.

"The FAA will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern."Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have informed Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with that operating system, instead opting for a previous version.

In rare circumstances where there is a missed approach — and where a pilot is using a precision approach with autopilot engaged and makes changes to their pre-programmed flight plan — an issue with the flight management computer could cause the plane's vertical navigation system, known as VNAV, to disengage and transition to a less sophisticated level of automated pitch control. The VNAV is essentially designed to automatically maintain the pre-planned altitude at various waypoints along a flight path.If this glitch occurs, however, pilots will need to take additional steps during their subsequent approach. "How busy do you want your crew to be?" one airline source told CBS News about the glitch. "Are you introducing distractions at the worst possible moment?""Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario," a Boeing spokesperson told CBS News in a statement. "We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue."The Boeing spokesperson said that even if VNAV disengages, autopilot will continue to function, adding that all pilots are trained to safely land without VNAV. In a bulletin sent to airlines late last month, Boeing told operators the glitch is not an immediate safety issue. It surfaced in versions 14 and 14.1 of the operating system for the Max's flight management computer. "The FAA is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain Boeing 737 MAX airplanes and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines," the FAA told CBS News in a statement. "The FAA will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern."Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have informed Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with that operating system, instead opting for a previous version. Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest and United told CBS News none of their in-service 737 Max fleets use the software version in question. CBS News has learned Boeing was first told of the issue by an airline in November 2024. The company reviewed it and determined in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. However, Boeing received what a source described as "additional information from operators" earlier this year that prompted the manufacturer to launch a formal safety review board. Boeing's initial bulletin told airlines a software fix would be ready sometime in 2028 and it would issue updated guidance about procedures for pilots to follow in November. The company is working to accelerate both of those efforts. The FAA review could further delay the certification of the 737 Max 10, the fourth and largest variant of the Max. The issue could also delay deliveries of the recently certified 737 Max 7. Nearly the entire order book for that aircraft is going to Southwest. The Max is a cash cow for Boeing and is vital for its turnaround efforts. The plane has been the subject of two high-profile crashes in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people due to defective software, and it experienced a mid-flight door panel blowout on an Alaska Airlines flight in January 2024 that was blamed on manufacturing mistakes. It is notable that several U.S. airlines appear to be taking a trust-but-verify approach to Boeing on the issue, having been stung by groundings and delays due to previous Boeing mistakes on the Max. The Max 7 was certified with software version 14, while the Max 10 was using version 14.1 during its certification testing. The software glitch was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. CBS News has also reached out to Allegiant Air for comment, which also operates the 737 Max.

extraction.body: Attackers are using compromised Ukrainian websites and fake Cloudflare checks to deliver Lunex, a malware-as-a-service platform that steals browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets and files. The campaign uses a vulnerable AMD driver to blind security tools before deploying the stealer. Attackers are using compromised Ukrainian websites to deliver Lunex, a malware-as-a-service platform that steals browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets and files from Windows systems. Victims first encounter a compromised website that displays a fake Cloudflare verification check. The page directs them toward an MSI installer that launches LunexLoader. LunexLoader uses the CMSTPLUA COM object to bypass User Account Control, then loads a vulnerable kernel driver from AMD Radeon Software. The driver, PDFWKRNL.sys , contains the flaw tracked as CVE-2023-20598 . The attackers use the driver in a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attack, or BYOVD. Instead of killing security processes, the malware uses kernel callbacks to interfere with their visibility while Windows keeps those processes running. Ontinue described the method as a quieter form of endpoint detection and response evasion. Ontinue testing found that Microsoft’s Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity and Vulnerable Driver Blocklist did not stop the specific driver variant in this campaign. The LOLRdrivers project cataloged the driver hash in March 2026, but detection by a public catalog did not prevent the malware from loading it. “The stealer extracts credentials and data from seven Chromium-based browsers,” Ontinue threat researcher Rhys Downing said in a technical report. Arctic Wolf Labs documented the wider campaign after finding injected iframes on legitimate websites operated by businesses in Ukraine. The affected sites included a hair-treatment clinic, a model manufacturer, a bookseller, a psychology facility, a tool retailer and an automotive retailer. After attackers disable security monitoring, LunexStealer contacts its command-and-control server at 193.178.159[.]128 over HTTP. The malware searches Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Yandex Browser, Opera, Opera GX and Vivaldi. It collects saved credentials, session cookies and browser data. It also searches for five desktop wallets: The stealer targets four browser wallet extensions as well: MetaMask, MetaMask Legacy, OKX Wallet and SafePal Wallet. Lunex creates persistence through a Registry Run key and a hidden scheduled task named psychedelicloveUtils . It also installs a Chrome Native Messaging Host, a mechanism that lets browser extensions communicate with programs on the computer. Chrome documents the feature in its Native Messaging guide . The host contains a 13,200-byte PowerShell script inside the malware’s .rdata section. The script communicates through standard input and output and can perform these file and system actions: The separate host can remain after someone deletes the main stealer binary. It can return after a reboot and reconnect when the victim restarts the browser. Lunex also modifies Chrome’s Secure Preferences to inject a malicious extension. The extension requests access to cookies, history, bookmarks, tabs, storage, proxy settings, scripting, declarative network requests and all HTTP and HTTPS URLs. Those permissions give the operators broad control over browser activity. Researchers first linked the name Lunex to the platform in June 2026, when BlueTeamCoolTeam researcher Luke Wilkinson identified six command-and-control panels in the United States, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Ukraine. Ontinue later identified 28 panels across 13 countries, including Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France, Germany, Turkey and Bangladesh. The researchers found evidence of a Russian-speaking developer or development team. The names Psychedelic Stealer and LunexStealer refer to the same victim-side malware. Psychedelic describes the executable file, while Lunex names the platform that criminal groups can use or buy. One panel in Turkey resolved to five phishing domains, including account-sams-club[.]com , teamwork-recover-password[.]com and whatsappbusineses[.]com . The infrastructure suggests that the platform supports brand impersonation and phishing as well as credential theft. Windows administrators should search for PDFWKRNL.sys , the psychedelicloveUtils scheduled task, unexpected Registry Run entries and unfamiliar Chrome Native Messaging Host registrations. Teams should treat those indicators as starting points because operators can change filenames, domains and infrastructure. Security teams should review driver inventories and use vendor-supported controls to block vulnerable kernel drivers. HVCI and Microsoft’s driver blocklist add useful protection, but Ontinue’s testing shows that defenders need layered controls when a campaign uses a driver variant that bypasses those safeguards. Organizations should manage browser extensions through policy, restrict native hosts to approved software and monitor changes to Chrome’s Secure Preferences. Endpoint telemetry should flag MSI files launched from browsers, PowerShell scripts that read and write arbitrary files, and browser processes that load unexpected extensions. If an infection occurs, responders should isolate the Windows device, revoke browser sessions, reset exposed passwords from a clean system and move cryptocurrency holdings to new wallets. Website owners should inspect content-management systems, review recently changed files and search for injected iframes that redirect visitors to fake verification pages. Kiteworks urged customers to take a nine-hour shutdown window over the weekend after federal intelligence authorities warned of a possible attack against some systems. The company said it has found no evidence of compromise and advised customers to install release 9.5.1. AI agents now touch sensitive data across browsers, cloud accounts, endpoints and SaaS tools. extraction.body: The Psychedelic Stealer malware distributed via compromised Ukrainian websites using ClickFix-style Cloudflare verification checks is part of a wider malware-as-a-service (MaaS) platform called Lunex . The new findings come from Ontinue, which described the activity as a four-stage attack chain aimed at targeting Ukrainian-speaking users. "The attack chain begins with a fake CAPTCHA page and culminates in the deployment of a fully-featured C2 agent," Ontinue threat researcher Rhys Downing said in a technical report. "The stealer extracts credentials and data from seven Chromium-based browsers, exfiltrates cryptocurrency wallets, and establishes persistent remote filesystem access through a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host installed within the victim's browser." The infection makes use of bogus MSI installers delivered via ClickFix to trigger a series of actions, including delivering a loader dubbed LunexLoader that's designed to bypass User Account Control (UAC) on Windows using the CMSTPLUA COM object, leverage the bring your own vulnerable driver ( BYOVD ) attack for defense evasion, and finally download the stealer payload. The use of the BYOVD technique is significant, not least because it's rarely employed as a precursor to a final-stage payload like an information stealer. Lunex takes advantage of a vulnerable kernel-mode driver for AMD Radeon Software ("PDFWKRNL.sys"), which is susceptible to CVE-2023-20598 , to escalate privileges and blind security-related processes while keeping them running. Psychedelic Stealer was first documented earlier this week by Arctic Wolf Labs, detailing the threat actor's modus operandi of compromising legitimate websites belonging to a hair-treatment clinic, a scale-model manufacturer, a specialist bookseller, a psychological facility, a tool retailer, and an automotive retailer to inject an iframe element designed to serve the ClickFix lure. "Our analysis of the attack chain found that, before the stealer is delivered, the malware is designed to use a legitimate but vulnerable driver to switch off security tools on the victim's machine. With those protections disabled, the information stealer is then deployed to take browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet data," Downing told The Hacker News. The earliest reference to Lunex in cybersecurity literature dates back to June 2026, when BlueTeamCoolTeam's Luke Wilkinson identified six active Lunex Stealer's command-and-control (C2) panels across the U.S., Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Ukraine. It's worth noting that both Psychedelic Stealer and LunexStealer refer to the same component of the MaaS platform. "'Psychedelic' is the name of the malware file that runs on victims' devices, while Lunex is the underlying platform being sold to multiple criminal groups, which is the reason for the name 'Lunex' and 'LunexStealer,'" Downing explained. Upon execution, LunexStealer communicates with the Lunex panel at 193.178.159[.]128 over HTTP to facilitate comprehensive information theft - "The host is backed by a 13,200-byte PowerShell script embedded in the .rdata section that implements the Chrome Native Messaging protocol over standard input and output," Downing said. "The NMH operates within Chrome’s process context. It survives stealer binary deletion, system reboots, and browser restarts." The PowerShell script supports six file system actions - What's more, LunexStealer injects a malicious Chrome extension by manipulating Chrome Secure Preferences and declares extensive permissions for cookies, history, bookmarks, tabs, storage, proxy, scripting, declarativeNetRequest, and all HTTP and HTTPS URLs. This grants the extension complete visibility and control over a victim's browser activity. Analysis of the Lunex panel points to a Russian-speaking developer or development team, with 28 unique panels identified across 13 countries, marking a major expansion from June 2026. These panels are hosted in Russia, the U.S., the U.K., the Netherlands, France, Germany, Turkey, and Bangladesh. "That growth in just a few months shows the platform is actively expanding and being used by either one threat actor or sold for other actors, not just a single operator," Downing said. One of the panels hosted in Turkey has been found to resolve to five phishing domains - This indicates that the MaaS platform's feature set extends beyond credential theft to also enable brand impersonation and phishing. "The BYOVD delivery chain, using PDB-guided kernel callback zeroing rather than process termination, represents a quieter approach to EDR neutralisation that leaves security products running but blind," Ontinue said. "Validated testing demonstrated that neither HVCI nor the current Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist prevents the specific PDFWKRNL.sys variant used in this chain from loading, a gap that persists despite the driver hash being catalogued in the LOLDrivers project since March 2026." Windows administrators should search for PDFWKRNL.sys , the psychedelicloveUtils scheduled task, unexpected Registry Run entries and unfamiliar Chrome Native Messaging Host registrations. Teams should treat those indicators as starting points because operators can change filenames, domains and infrastructure.

Security teams should review driver inventories and use vendor-supported controls to block vulnerable kernel drivers. HVCI and Microsoft’s driver blocklist add useful protection, but Ontinue’s testing shows that defenders need layered controls when a campaign uses a driver variant that bypasses those safeguards.

Website owners should inspect content-management systems, review recently changed files and search for injected iframes that redirect visitors to fake verification pages.

extraction.body: The Psychedelic Stealer malware distributed via compromised Ukrainian websites using ClickFix-style Cloudflare verification checks is part of a wider malware-as-a-service (MaaS) platform called Lunex . The new findings come from Ontinue, which described the activity as a four-stage attack chain aimed at targeting Ukrainian-speaking users. "The attack chain begins with a fake CAPTCHA page and culminates in the deployment of a fully-featured C2 agent," Ontinue threat researcher Rhys Downing said in a technical report. "The stealer extracts credentials and data from seven Chromium-based browsers, exfiltrates cryptocurrency wallets, and establishes persistent remote filesystem access through a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host installed within the victim's browser." The infection makes use of bogus MSI installers delivered via ClickFix to trigger a series of actions, including delivering a loader dubbed LunexLoader that's designed to bypass User Account Control (UAC) on Windows using the CMSTPLUA COM object, leverage the bring your own vulnerable driver ( BYOVD ) attack for defense evasion, and finally download the stealer payload. The use of the BYOVD technique is significant, not least because it's rarely employed as a precursor to a final-stage payload like an information stealer. Lunex takes advantage of a vulnerable kernel-mode driver for AMD Radeon Software ("PDFWKRNL.sys"), which is susceptible to CVE-2023-20598 , to escalate privileges and blind security-related processes while keeping them running. Psychedelic Stealer was first documented earlier this week by Arctic Wolf Labs, detailing the threat actor's modus operandi of compromising legitimate websites belonging to a hair-treatment clinic, a scale-model manufacturer, a specialist bookseller, a psychological facility, a tool retailer, and an automotive retailer to inject an iframe element designed to serve the ClickFix lure. "Our analysis of the attack chain found that, before the stealer is delivered, the malware is designed to use a legitimate but vulnerable driver to switch off security tools on the victim's machine. With those protections disabled, the information stealer is then deployed to take browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet data," Downing told The Hacker News. The earliest reference to Lunex in cybersecurity literature dates back to June 2026, when BlueTeamCoolTeam's Luke Wilkinson identified six active Lunex Stealer's command-and-control (C2) panels across the U.S., Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Ukraine. It's worth noting that both Psychedelic Stealer and LunexStealer refer to the same component of the MaaS platform. "'Psychedelic' is the name of the malware file that runs on victims' devices, while Lunex is the underlying platform being sold to multiple criminal groups, which is the reason for the name 'Lunex' and 'LunexStealer,'" Downing explained. Upon execution, LunexStealer communicates with the Lunex panel at 193.178.159[.]128 over HTTP to facilitate comprehensive information theft - "The host is backed by a 13,200-byte PowerShell script embedded in the .rdata section that implements the Chrome Native Messaging protocol over standard input and output," Downing said. "The NMH operates within Chrome’s process context. It survives stealer binary deletion, system reboots, and browser restarts." The PowerShell script supports six file system actions - What's more, LunexStealer injects a malicious Chrome extension by manipulating Chrome Secure Preferences and declares extensive permissions for cookies, history, bookmarks, tabs, storage, proxy, scripting, declarativeNetRequest, and all HTTP and HTTPS URLs. This grants the extension complete visibility and control over a victim's browser activity. Analysis of the Lunex panel points to a Russian-speaking developer or development team, with 28 unique panels identified across 13 countries, marking a major expansion from June 2026. These panels are hosted in Russia, the U.S., the U.K., the Netherlands, France, Germany, Turkey, and Bangladesh. "That growth in just a few months shows the platform is actively expanding and being used by either one threat actor or sold for other actors, not just a single operator," Downing said. One of the panels hosted in Turkey has been found to resolve to five phishing domains - This indicates that the MaaS platform's feature set extends beyond credential theft to also enable brand impersonation and phishing. "The BYOVD delivery chain, using PDB-guided kernel callback zeroing rather than process termination, represents a quieter approach to EDR neutralisation that leaves security products running but blind," Ontinue said. "Validated testing demonstrated that neither HVCI nor the current Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist prevents the specific PDFWKRNL.sys variant used in this chain from loading, a gap that persists despite the driver hash being catalogued in the LOLDrivers project since March 2026." extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (WFLA) — Federal prosecutors have indicted two people in the incident involving an explosive device left at MacDill Air Force Base. According to Greg Kehoe, U.S. attorney for the Middle District of Florida, Alen Zheng has been accused of attempting to "damage or destroy" the Visitor's Center at the Dale Mabry Gate with an improvised explosive device, also known as an IED. The defendant attempted to detonate the device on March 10, but it did not explode, officials said. Minutes later, a 911 call was made saying there was an explosive planted at MacDill Air Force Base, but it did not specify the location. Kehoe said after planting the bomb, the suspect and his sister sold the car Alen Zheng used to plant the explosive to CarMax and bought tickets to flee to China. "Although the vehicle had been vacuumed and had been cleaned, there were traces of items that were residue for the IED, and it was consistent with the IED that was picked up," Kehoe said. And of course, immediately thereafter, the lab reports came back notifying law enforcement that this was, in fact, an improvised explosive device." By March 12, both siblings were in China, although Ann-Mary Zheng later returned to the Tampa Bay area by March 18. On March 16, MacDill AFB security found the explosive device and immediately contacted law enforcement. "Less than 24 hours later, the agents identified the IMEI number for the phone used in the 911 call, and those of you familiar with the IMEI number, it's an international mobile environment identification number," Kehoe said. "These agents and law enforcement officers then got the film from Best Buy," Kehoe said. In conjunction with that, at literally the same time, law enforcement, TPD and other entities were identifying the vehicle and placing it at that location on the evening of March 10." Alen Zheng was charged with attempted damage of government property by fire or explosion, unlawful making of a destructive device, and possession of unregistered destructive device. However, he has remained in China as of this report. Ann-Mary Zheng was not charged in the incident directly but was accused of tampering with evidence, including a 2010 black Mercedes-Benz GLK 350. She was arrested and indicted for accessory after the fact and evidence tampering.

sources.title: One person detained following security breach at MacDill Air Force Base
passages: Base security personnel detained an unauthorized civilian who breached the perimeter of MacDill Air Force Base and violently fought responding officers Saturday afternoon, according to officials. A civilian intruder without authorized access breached the base boundary around 1 p.m.
It also remains unclear how the civilian managed to bypass the perimeter barrier.Law enforcement authorities are actively investigating the security breach.

Security officers responded quickly, and the assailant violently engaged them before being taken into custody, according to the base. Officials state both the assailant and an officer received non-life-threatening injuries during the physical struggle.
